en: The Sūtra on the Ten Dreams of the King of Śrāvastī Spoken by the Buddha;
appended to the Records of the Western Jin.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in a monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a king named...
Prasenajit had ten dreams one night:
first, there were three cauldrons; the boiling vapors from the two side cauldrons rose up and mingled with one another, yet they did not enter the empty central cauldron.
Second, the king dreamed that a horse was eating from both its mouth and its rump.
Third, he saw a great tree blooming with flowers.
Fourth, he saw a small tree bearing fruit.
Fifth, he saw a man cutting a rope with a knife; behind the man was a sheep, which was eating the rope.
Sixth, he saw a Hu barbarian sitting on a bed of gold and silver, eating from vessels of gold and silver.
Seventh, he saw a large mother cow returning to suckle her calf.

Eighth, he saw a herd of oxen running and lowing from the four directions, rushing toward one another as if to fight; just as they were about to collide, they vanished, and their whereabouts could not be known.
Ninth, he saw a large pond whose water was turbid in the center and clear at the four edges.
Tenth, he saw the water of a mountain stream as crimson.
Upon waking from his dream, the king was struck with terror, fearing for the loss of his kingdom and his own life.
The next day, he immediately summoned his attendants, ministers, and various heterodox practitioners, saying:
"Last night I saw ten things in a dream; who among you can interpret them?
A certain heterodox practitioner replied:
"I am able to explain it, but I fear that if Your Majesty hears it,
you will not be pleased. The King said, "Speak then, according to what you know."
The heterodox practitioner said, "The King shall lose his kingdom and his life.
The King was greatly alarmed and terrified; did he not find this unbearable? The heterodox practitioner said:

"It is loathsome; you must kill the crown prince and the queen you hold dear, and burn all their treasuries to offer as a sacrifice to the gods. If the King can do this, he shall remain free from misfortune."

When the king heard the words of the practitioner, he was filled with grief, bewilderment, and alarm; distressed and finding no joy, he withdrew into his chamber of purification to contemplate this matter.
The king had a queen named Māri, who went to the chamber of purification and asked:
"Why has Your Majesty entered the chamber of purification during the day? Your countenance is not serene and you are so deeply distressed; who has committed an offense against Your Majesty?"
The King replied, "Do not question this matter; you are merely afraid and timid, for it is beyond your understanding. The Queen said:
"I am the very body of the King; you must inform me when there is something urgent.
The King then spoke to his consort, saying:
"Last night I saw ten things in a dream. I consulted a master of dreams, who interpreted them for me thus. I am deeply terrified and do not know whom to tell."
The lady said: "Do not be anxious or sorrowful.

It is like a person who buys gold and rubs it upon a stone to see for himself its quality; now that the Buddha is nearby at the vihāra, you may go and ask him, and all calamities and wonders will be known."
The next day, the king immediately summoned several thousand of his most eminent ministers and went to where the Buddha was staying. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, the king said:
“Regarding the ten matters I dreamed of last night, I pray that the Buddha will explain them for me.”
The Buddha told the king:
"Do not be anxious or grieved!
That which you dreamed was merely a manifestation of future events."
The Buddha said:

“As for the King’s dream of seeing three cauldrons, with the steam from the two side cauldrons rising and mingling while not entering the empty central cauldron—this signifies that in future generations, people will no longer provide for their poor relatives or the solitary and orphaned, but instead the wealthy will only exchange gifts among themselves. This is precisely what the King has seen in his first dream.”

As for the King’s dream that a horse eats from both its mouth and its rump: in future generations, high ministers and senior officials will receive stipends from the state and yet also consume the resources of the people; they will even consume those who are wronged. The two things seen in the King’s dream refer precisely to this.

As for the King’s dream of a great tree blooming with flowers: it means that in future generations, people will have white hair on their heads before they have even reached the age of thirty. These three things seen in the King’s dream refer precisely to this.

As for the king’s dream of a small tree bearing fruit, it refers precisely to this: that in future generations, women who have not yet reached the age of fifteen will marry and carry infants, without knowing shame or modesty. This is the meaning of the fourth matter seen in the king’s dream.

The King saw in his dream a man cutting a rope, behind whom was a sheep; the sheep then proceeded to eat the rope. This refers precisely to women in future generations: when a husband must go into service or travel for trade, the wife remains behind and takes a man into her bed, consuming her husband’s wealth. These five things seen in the King’s dream are exactly this.

As for the King’s dream of the Hu barbarians feasting on gold and silver beds using gold and silver vessels: it means that in future generations, those who are noble shall become base, and those who are base shall become noble; those in high positions shall sit and consume rich delicacies, while the gentleman shall eat dregs and husks, and the commoner shall eat fine rice. That the King saw these six matters in his dream is precisely for this reason.

As for the king’s dream of a great ox returning to suckle from its own calf: in future generations, mothers will act as matchmakers for their daughters, bringing other men to share a chamber with them; the mother will then guard the door and collect wealth to support herself. This seventh matter seen in the king’s dream refers precisely to this.

The King dreamed that a herd of oxen came bellowing from the four directions, rushing toward one another as if about to fight; just as they were about to clash, they vanished, and their whereabouts were unknown. This signifies that in future generations, those who are greedy and lustful will keep many wives, causing the king, his ministers, the common people, and the elders all to rejoice greatly. Whether such things will occur in the present or future life, in an instant the clouds dispersed. At that moment, beholding this marvel, the King wished to cause people to fear the prohibitions of Heaven and Earth, so that they might cease their greed and lust, guard their own wives with compassion, and eliminate the harm caused by others' wives. These eight matters seen in the King’s dream are precisely for this purpose.

"The King saw in his dream a large pond whose water was turbid in the center and clear at the four edges; this signifies that in future generations, people within the kingdom will not revere their elders, but shall instead revere the youths of bordering states. This is precisely what is meant by the ninth matter seen in the King's dream."

As for the King’s dream that the waters of a great ravine were perfectly crimson: this refers to the fact that in future generations, ministers and high officials will know no bounds in their desires; they will raise armies and gather multitudes to attack and subdue one another, slaughtering the people until the blood flows so red as to dye the water crimson. This is precisely what the King’s tenth dream portends.
"O King, do not fear, do not fear!
There shall be no harm to your kingdom, to your person, or to your wife and children; these dreams are all portents of matters yet to come in future lives.
The king then knelt upright and said:

"Upon attaining the Buddha's teaching, the mind immediately rejoices; it is like a person holding a small vessel to receive oil: when the oil is abundant and the vessel small, they seek a larger vessel; having obtained the large vessel, they receive more of it, and thus become secure and free from fear."
The king immediately prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, bowed twice, and departed.

Returning to the palace, he bestowed further gifts upon his principal consort, confiscated the stipends of all the high officials and great ministers, and no longer placed faith in the words of the Brahmins.
The Sūtra on the Ten Dreams of the King of Śrāvastī Spoken by the Buddha.
